summary: Mabel Veronica Batten, a singer known as 'Ladye', was Radclyffe Hall's first lover. The Ransom Center's biographical sketch credits her with introducing Hall into a circle of artistic and intellectual women, many of them lesbians - so she is, in the surviving record, the person who brought Hall into queer society. Batten was also the cousin of Una Troubridge, who met Hall in 1915 and became Hall's partner after Batten's death the following year; the three-way relation gave Hall's biographer Michael Baker his title, Our Three Selves.

sources.quote: Hall's first lover, singer and society beauty Mabel Veronica Batten (1856-1916), introduced her into a circle of artistic and intellectual women, many of them lesbians.
sources.context: The Harry Ransom Center's Biographical Sketch in the finding aid to the Hall and Troubridge papers (eadid 00163), under the heading 'Radclyffe Hall (1880-1943)'. The next sentence introduces Troubridge as Batten's cousin. Apostrophes rendered straight, as in the source HTML.
sources.supports: That Batten was Hall's first lover, her dates, and her role in bringing Hall into queer society.

sources.quote: While we cannot know for certain what grief John writes of here, it seems likely that the reference is to the death of Mabel Veronica Batten (Ladye), which occurred when John was in the first throes of her passion for Una, a passion very similar to that John was now feeling for Souline. The irony, of course, is that Ladye was grieved by that passion, just as Una was now grieved.
sources.context: Joanne Glasgow's editorial footnote to Hall's letter to Evguenia Souline of 27 July 1934, glossing Hall's own sentence on the same page - 'I slept, Soulina, as once before in my life I slept as the result of a fearful grief'. Note the hedge: Glasgow does not claim to know, and says so first. This is the editor writing about Hall, not Hall writing about Batten, and it is recorded as such.
sources.supports: An editor's reading that Hall's worst remembered grief was Batten's death, and that Batten was grieved by Hall's passion for Troubridge - second-hand, hedged, and the only thing in this volume that bears on this pair.
sources.citation_provenance: PDF p. 7 (printed pp. 28-29; folio 29 in the running head)
sources.speaker: Joanne Glasgow, ed.

sources.quote: What is clear is that the two women who left England as friends came back as lovers. From this time onwards they would rarely be out of each other's company. The date they crossed the Channel to Ostend was August 12, John's birthday. Ever afterwards this anniversary became a double celebration.
sources.context: Baker on the summer 1908 Belgian holiday. Hall and Batten had met at Homburg on 22 August 1907 - Batten fifty and married, Hall twenty-seven - and both women kept that date as an anniversary too.
sources.supports: Biographer's full account of the Batten relationship, including its start.

null_findings.finding: The words 'Ladye', 'Mabel' and 'Batten' occur on one page only - printed 29 - and only in Glasgow's footnote. The copy used is a 30-page extract, not the whole book (printed folios run 32 to 80 plus front matter), so this is not a whole-volume null; and the volume is by nature a Hall-to-Souline source. Hall's testimony about Batten, if anywhere, is in the Troubridge diaries at the Harry Ransom Center.
